chapter_title: Interacting with Smart Contracts from the Frontend

screens.title: Interacting with Smart Contracts from the Frontend
screens.subtitle: How the ABI, Provider, Signer, and ethers.Contract enable your DApp to read state, send transactions, and react to events.

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn how a frontend actually speaks to a deployed smart contract. We begin with the contract ABI, the structured JSON blueprint that tells your application the names, inputs, outputs, and events a contract exposes. You will see how that ABI combines with a contract address and an Ethereum provider to create an ethers. js Contract object for read-only operations. Then we move to state-changing calls, where a signer authorizes transactions and you wait for confirmations with a transaction receipt. Listening for events enables real-time UI updates without heavy polling. Practical topics include common errors like missing signer, incorrect ABI or address, and how to provide clear feedback to users. Finally, we'll connect these pieces inside a React component pattern that reads a value, sends an update, listens for an event, and cleans up listeners on unmount. By the end, you will understand not just the A P I calls but the user experience trade-offs and the safety practices needed to build a responsive DApp. What part of the contract interaction feels most unfamiliar to you right now?

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Frontend code needs the ABI, address, and a provider or signer to interact correctly with a deployed contract. These pieces let your DApp read state, send transactions, and react to events in a predictable, user-friendly way.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives frame the skills you will practice. First, you will be able to explain what the contract ABI is and why it is necessary for any frontend to encode calls and decode responses. Second, you will instantiate an ethers. js Contract using three pieces: the deployed address, the ABI, and either a provider or a signer. Third, you will call view or pure functions safely using a provider and understand why no gas is consumed for those reads. Fourth, you will send state-changing transactions by connecting a signer, monitoring the transaction hash, waiting for the mined confirmation, and updating the UI accordingly. Each objective pairs a technical step with a simple reason why it matters to the end user: correct encoding prevents errors, a signer protects private keys, waiting for confirmation keeps the UI consistent, and listening for events makes the app responsive. Expect concrete examples and a hands-on activity that deploys a Greeter contract locally and integrates it into a React component. This will help you move from concept to working DApp confidently.

screens.title: What is the Contract ABI?
screens.subtitle: The JSON blueprint that enables correct encoding and decoding

narration.text: The Contract Application Binary Interface, commonly called the ABI, is a machine-readable JSON array that describes a contract's public surface. It lists the constructor, each function's inputs and outputs, state mutability, and events. The ABI does not contain the contract's bytecode or state; instead, it tells a frontend how to format calls and how to interpret return values and event arguments. For example, a Greeter contract exposes a greet function that returns a string and a setGreeting function that takes a single string argument and emits a NewGreeting event. The ABI entry for greet describes its output type so your code can decode a returned string. This matters because without a correct ABI your frontend would produce malformed calldata or misread responses, leading to cryptic errors. A common misconception is to think the ABI is optional; it is required whenever you want to call or listen to a contract from JavaScript. In practice compilers produce the ABI after compilation, and the deployment process copies that ABI into your frontend project. A useful check is to ensure the ABI matches the deployed contract; if you redeploy a changed contract and forget to update the frontend ABI, calls will fail or return unexpected data. Takeaway: treat the ABI as the contract's public contract with your frontend.

keyIdea.title: ABI is essential
keyIdea.text: The ABI defines the contract's public interface and is required to encode calls and decode responses correctly.

content.html:
Core Concept

What is the Contract ABI?

A JSON array that describes every callable function and event of a compiled contract.

ABI example (simplified)
[
  { "name": "greet", "type": "function", "stateMutability": "view", "outputs": [{"type": "string"}] },
  { "name": "setGreeting", "type": "function", "inputs": [{"type": "string"}], "stateMutability": "nonpayable" },
  { "name": "NewGreeting", "type": "event", "inputs": [{"indexed": true, "type": "address"}, {"type": "string"}] }
]
This structure tells your frontend how to encode parameters, which calls are view-only, and how to decode events.
Why it matters
  • Without a matching ABI, calldata will be mis-encoded and calls will fail.
  • The ABI indicates which functions are read-only versus state-changing.
  • Events in the ABI let frontends decode emitted event arguments for live updates.
Concrete example
After compiling Greeter, copy the generated ABI JSON into your frontend. Use that ABI when instantiating an ethers.Contract so greet returns the expected string.
Key Takeaway

The ABI is the contract's public interface. Keep it in sync with deployed code.

screens.title: Provider and Signer
screens.subtitle: Roles: reading state versus signing transactions

narration.text: Understanding the provider and the signer is central to interacting with contracts. A provider is an ethers. js object that connects to an Ethereum node and allows read-only operations. When you call view or pure functions you only need a provider; these calls are executed locally on the node and consume no gas. A signer is an abstraction for an account that can sign transactions. When you want to change state, the frontend must connect a signer to the contract so the wallet prompts the user to authorize the transaction and cover gas. In code this looks like creating a Contract with a provider for reads and then connecting it to a signer for writes. A common pitfall is trying to send a state-changing call on a contract instantiated with only a provider; this produces a missing signer error. Another important detail is where you obtain the provider and signer: injected wallets like MetaMask expose a bridge object that you can wrap with ethers' provider. In a React DApp you often keep the provider in state and derive the signer after the user connects. This separation keeps read operations available before the user signs in, and transfers the responsibility for private keys to the wallet rather than your frontend. Reflect: which actions in your UI should be allowed before a user connects a wallet?

keyIdea.title: Provider vs Signer
keyIdea.text: Use a Provider for reads and a Signer for state changes; never attempt to sign transactions without a signer attached.

content.html:
Definition

Provider and Signer

Provider connects to a node for reads; Signer authorizes transactions and pays gas.

Provider (read-only)
Connects to an Ethereum node, lets you call view and pure functions without gas. Use it to fetch contract state and block data.
  • No signer required for reads.
  • Good for showing public data before user connects.
Signer (write-enabled)
Represents an account able to sign transactions. A wallet provides the signer so private keys never touch your frontend code.
  • Required for state-changing calls and gas payment.
  • Prompting the wallet is a user consent step.
Concrete integration pattern
// provider for reads
const contract = new ethers.Contract(address, abi, provider);
// connect signer for writes
const contractWithSigner = contract.connect(signer);
const tx = await contractWithSigner.setGreeting("Hi");
await tx.wait();
Common mistake

Attempting a write call with a contract that only has a provider will throw a missing signer error. Always connect the signer before sending transactions.

screens.title: Instantiate ethers.Contract
screens.subtitle: Address, ABI, Provider/Signer — the three required pieces

narration.text: Creating an ethers. js Contract instance is a simple and powerful step. You need three things: the contract address where the bytecode lives, the contract ABI that describes the interface, and an ethers Provider or a Signer depending on whether you plan to read or write. In practice you often import a JSON file containing both the compiled ABI and the deployed address from your deployment script. For read-only behavior instantiate the Contract with the provider so you can call view functions directly. When you need to send transactions, call connect with a signer to obtain a contract instance capable of sending signed transactions. A clear pattern in React is to create the contract when the provider becomes available, keep it in component state, then connect a signer only when a user is authenticated. A misconception is to duplicate contract instances for reads and writes unnecessarily; you can reuse the same base contract and call connect with different signers as needed. Always validate that the address matches the network you are connected to. If you attempt to call a contract at the wrong address or on a different network, you will either receive empty results or RPC errors. The practical tip: keep ABI and address together in a JSON file and import them into your frontend to avoid mismatches.

keyIdea.title: Three required pieces
keyIdea.text: Instantiate a Contract with address, ABI, and provider. Connect a signer for writes using contract.connect(signer).

content.html:
Process Flow

Instantiate ethers.Contract

Use the address, ABI, and a provider or signer to make a callable contract object.

Code pattern
import GreeterJson from '../abi/Greeter.json';
const address = GreeterJson.address;
const abi = GreeterJson.abi;
const contract = new ethers.Contract(address, abi, provider);
// Later, to send a transaction:
const contractWithSigner = contract.connect(signer);
const tx = await contractWithSigner.setGreeting(value);
await tx.wait();
Practical checks
  • Confirm the contract address matches the network.
  • Use the ABI produced by the same compiler output as the deployed bytecode.
  • Reuse the base contract and call connect for different signers instead of recreating objects repeatedly.
Concrete example
Place Greeter.json in src/abi, import it, then instantiate with provider to fetch the greeting immediately on page load.
Key Takeaway

Address + ABI + Provider/Signer = a usable Contract. Keep ABI and address in sync with deployed code.

screens.title: Calling Read-Only Functions
screens.subtitle: Use a provider to fetch contract state without gas

narration.text: Read-only functions in Solidity, marked view or pure, do not change blockchain state and therefore do not consume gas. From the frontend you call these functions directly on a Contract instance that was created with an ethers Provider. The provider will query a node and return the value, which your code can render immediately. A typical example is the greet function that returns a stored string. Because reads do not require a signer, you can display contract data before the user connects a wallet. This improves perceived performance and lowers friction. However, note that provider responses depend on the node you connect to; an out-of-date or misconfigured node could return stale data. If consistent, real-time accuracy is critical you might subscribe to events or fetch the latest block first. Another misconception is thinking that calling view functions is instantaneous or always reliable; network latency and provider rate limits can affect response times. Implement try-catch around reads and surface friendly messages when data cannot be fetched. Also consider what should happen in your UI when the contract returns empty or unexpected values — provide sensible defaults and clear recovery paths for users.

keyIdea.title: Reads are gas-free
keyIdea.text: View and pure functions are called with a Provider and do not require a signer or gas. Handle node latency and errors gracefully.

content.html:
Definition

Calling Read-Only Functions

Use a Provider to call view or pure functions without sending a transaction.

Example: fetch greeting
const contract = new ethers.Contract(address, abi, provider);
const greeting = await contract.greet();
setCurrentGreeting(greeting);
No wallet prompt appears and no gas is used. This call reads the node's state and returns a decoded string because the ABI describes the output.
Best practices & pitfalls
  • Wrap reads in try-catch to surface friendly errors if the node is unreachable.
  • Provide a loading state and sensible defaults if data is temporarily unavailable.
  • Be mindful of provider rate limits when polling; rely on events when possible.
Concrete scenario
In Greeter, show the current greeting using a provider so visitors see the value immediately without connecting a wallet. Offer a connect button only for writes.

screens.title: Sending State-Changing Transactions
screens.subtitle: Connect a signer, send the tx, and wait for confirmation

narration.text: State-changing functions require a signer because the user must authorize the transaction and pay gas. The typical flow is: connect your wallet to get a signer, connect that signer to your Contract instance, call the function which returns a transaction object, and then await the transaction confirmation with the wait method. Waiting is crucial — sending the transaction only means it was submitted to the network. Until the transaction is mined and confirmed, the on-chain state may not reflect the intended change. In a React DApp you should show a clear progression: transaction sent with the hash, waiting for confirmation, and then confirmed with a receipt. Also handle user rejection gracefully: when a user rejects in MetaMask you will get a specific error code; catch that and inform the user rather than surfacing raw RPC errors. Gas management is another concern: ensure users have enough ETH for fees and show estimated costs when possible. Avoid automatically retrying failed transactions without user action. A common misconception is to assume tx. wait is instantaneous; confirmations take time and your UI should remain responsive during this period. Use optimistic UI updates carefully, paired with events or a confirmed receipt to reconcile state.

keyIdea.title: Wait for tx confirmation
keyIdea.text: Send state-changing calls with a signer, then await tx.wait() to obtain a reliable transaction receipt before trusting on-chain changes.

content.html:
Process Flow

Sending State-Changing Transactions

Connect signer, send the transaction, and wait for the receipt to ensure the on-chain change succeeded.

Typical sequence
  1. Request wallet connection to get signer.
  2. const contractWithSigner = contract.connect(signer).
  3. const tx = await contractWithSigner.setGreeting(value).
  4. Show tx.hash and await tx.wait() for confirmation.
User experience guidance
  • Inform the user when MetaMask opens and what they are signing.
  • Show the transaction hash so users can verify status externally if desired.
  • Disable repeated submissions while waiting for confirmation.
Common mistake
Assuming a transaction is final as soon as it's sent. Always await confirmation to ensure on-chain state matches your UI.

screens.title: Listening for Events
screens.subtitle: React to emitted events for real-time UI updates

narration.text: Events are logs emitted by smart contracts that provide a lightweight way to notify off-chain applications of changes. Listening for events is far more efficient than constant polling for many use cases. In ethers. js you attach a listener with contract. on and remove it with contract. off to avoid memory leaks. For example, Greeter emits NewGreeting when setGreeting runs; the frontend can listen for that event and immediately update the displayed greeting without waiting for a manual refetch. However, remember that events are not a replacement for confirmations: events are emitted during transaction processing and you should still verify the transaction receipt for critical flows. In React, attach listeners in an effect when the contract exists and clean them up on unmount. A common mistake is to attach multiple listeners during repeated renders, causing duplicate callbacks; always ensure your effect dependency array and cleanup are correct. Another important detail is that events can be replayed if you re-initiate listeners across page loads, so design idempotent handlers. Use events to reduce latency in the UI and provide a more interactive user experience, while still relying on confirmed receipts for authoritative state.

keyIdea.title: Events for live updates
keyIdea.text: Use contract.on to listen for events and update the UI in real time, but clean up listeners to prevent duplicates and rely on confirmations for critical logic.

content.html:
Core Concept

Listening for Events

Attach listeners to react to contract-emitted events for a responsive UI.

Example handler
contract.on('NewGreeting', (setter, newText, event) => {
  setStatusMessage(`New greeting "${newText}" set by ${setter}`);
  setCurrentGreeting(newText);
});
// cleanup: contract.off('NewGreeting')
Update the UI immediately when the event arrives and clean up the listener when the component unmounts.
Practical notes
  • Use events to avoid frequent polling.
  • Always off-load listeners on cleanup to prevent duplicates.
  • Design handlers to be idempotent in case of replays or duplicate events.
Concrete example
When NewGreeting fires, update the displayed greeting and show a status message indicating who set it. The event gives the setter address and the newText argument.

screens.title: Robust Error Handling
screens.subtitle: Catch, interpret, and present errors for a friendly DApp UX

narration.text: Errors are inevitable when interacting with remote nodes, wallets, and the blockchain itself. Your DApp should catch errors at every interaction point and translate them into actionable messages. Some common cases are user rejected transactions, insufficient funds for gas, RPC node failures, contract reverts, and mismatched ABI or address. A recommended pattern is to wrap async calls in try-catch blocks, inspect known error codes such as the wallet's user rejection code, and provide a next step for the user. For example, when the wallet returns a code indicating the user rejected the transaction, show a message that the transaction was cancelled rather than a raw stack trace. When a contract revert occurs, attempt to extract the revert reason if available and advise the user about possible causes. Avoid exposing internal error objects directly in the UI. Another practical tip is to anticipate network issues by showing retry affordances and offline states. In development, log detailed errors to the console for debugging, but keep production-facing messages concise and helpful. Finally, test error paths deliberately by rejecting transactions and simulating node outages so your UI behaves gracefully in real situations.

keyIdea.title: Handle errors gracefully
keyIdea.text: Use try-catch, interpret known wallet and RPC error codes, and show user-friendly messages and recovery options.

content.html:
Definition

Robust Error Handling

Translate raw errors into clear user actions and avoid exposing diagnostics to end users.

Common errors
  • User rejected transaction (wallet error code 4001).
  • Insufficient funds to cover gas fees.
  • Missing signer when attempting a write.
  • Incorrect ABI or contract address leading to decoding errors.
Handling pattern
try {
  const tx = await contractWithSigner.setGreeting(value);
  await tx.wait();
} catch (err) {
  if (err.code === 4001) setStatus('Transaction rejected by user.');
  else setStatus('Transaction failed: ' + (err.message || 'Unknown error'));
}
Map known codes to friendly messages, log for developers, and provide retry instructions when appropriate.

screens.title: Deploying Greeter and Saving ABI
screens.subtitle: A repeatable Hardhat deploy workflow for frontend integration

narration.text: A reliable development practice is to deploy locally, then save the contract address and ABI into your frontend project so the UI can interact with the exact deployed instance. Using Hardhat, compile your contracts and run the deploy script which prints the deployed address. The deploy script can also write a JSON file containing both the address and the ABI into your frontend's src/abi directory. This makes it easy to import the JSON in React and instantiate a Contract with confidence that the address and ABI match. When you redeploy after contract changes, repeat this step to update the frontend artifacts. A common mistake is to hardcode an address in a component without updating it after redeploying. Also confirm that the wallet network matches the network you deployed to; otherwise MetaMask will prevent interactions or produce confusing errors. In team environments, consider a simple script to inject the correct ABI and address into your development server on each deploy. This creates a reproducible loop: compile, deploy, copy ABI and address, run the frontend, and test read and write flows locally. The hands-on activity follows exactly this flow so you practice each step end to end.

keyIdea.title: Deployment plumbing
keyIdea.text: Save compiled ABI and deployed address into your frontend project after deploy so the UI can instantiate the correct Contract instance.

content.html:
Process Flow

Deploying Greeter and Saving ABI

Deploy locally with Hardhat and copy ABI and address into src/abi for the frontend to import.

Deployment script pattern
// after deploying
fs.writeFileSync('src/abi/Greeter.json', JSON.stringify({ address: greeter.target, abi: JSON.parse(greeter.interface.formatJson()) }, null, 2));
This keeps address and ABI together for straightforward import into your React app.
Checklist
  • Confirm Hardhat node is running when deploying locally.
  • Copy the deployed address into the frontend artifact.
  • Ensure the frontend and wallet use the same network.

screens.title: Integrating Contract Interaction into React
screens.subtitle: Component patterns: useEffect, state, and cleanup

narration.text: Integrating contract calls into React components requires careful state and lifecycle management. A common pattern is to create the Contract instance inside an effect that runs when the provider becomes available, fetch initial read-only data, and set up event listeners. Keep the contract object in component state so it can be reused for both reads and writes. When the user connects a wallet, obtain the signer and create a connected contract via contract. connect(signer) just before sending the transaction. Use another effect to register event listeners and return a cleanup function that removes them with contract. off to avoid memory leaks. Provide status messages for each asynchronous step: fetching data, sending transaction, waiting for confirmation, and confirmed. A frequent mistake is attaching listeners on every render; ensure your effect dependency arrays are correct so listeners are attached only when the contract reference changes. If you expect multiple components to use the same contract, lift the contract into context or a higher-level state so you avoid duplicate connections. This pattern makes your UI predictable: no repeated requests, clear lifecycle for listeners, and a straightforward path for upgrades and testing.

keyIdea.title: React lifecycle pattern
keyIdea.text: Instantiate contracts in effects, keep in state, connect signers on demand, and clean up listeners to avoid leaks and duplicates.

content.html:
Process Flow

Integrating Contract Interaction into React

Use effects to create contracts, fetch data, register listeners, and clean up on unmount.

Pattern summary
  1. Create provider and contract in an effect when provider exists.
  2. Fetch initial data and set state.
  3. Register event listeners and return cleanup to remove them.
  4. Connect signer only when sending transactions.
Concrete example notes
In the GreeterInteraction component, the effect checks for provider and ABI, creates a contract, fetches the greeting, and sets up a NewGreeting listener. The cleanup detaches the listener to avoid duplicate updates when the component unmounts or the provider changes.
Developer tip
Keep contracts in a shared context if multiple components need access. This centralizes listeners and reduces re-instantiation overhead.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.subtitle: Avoid ABI mismatches, missing signer, and unsafe practices

narration.text: This lesson collects the most frequent mistakes and safety reminders when integrating smart contracts into frontends. First, ABI or contract address mismatches are a primary cause of confusing errors; always deploy and copy the ABI and address from the same compilation output. Second, attempting writes without a signer will produce missing signer or permission errors; ensure your UI prevents write flows until a wallet is connected. Third, never hardcode private keys or sign transactions in the frontend — always rely on injected wallets to protect private keys. Fourth, provide clear messages for insufficient gas or user-rejected transactions rather than exposing raw error objects. Fifth, clean up event listeners to avoid duplicated handlers and memory leaks. Also be mindful of network configuration: the wallet must be pointed at the same network you deployed to. Finally, for security, avoid displaying or trusting unchecked contract data in sensitive contexts and validate user inputs before sending them to the contract. Testing error paths locally and deliberately rejecting transactions in the wallet will help you build a resilient UI that handles real user behavior gracefully.

keyIdea.title: Avoid these errors
keyIdea.text: Keep ABI and address in sync, require signer for writes, never embed private keys in frontend code, and always handle errors politely.

content.html:
Core Concept

Common Mistakes and Safety Notes

Quick comparison of frequent errors and how to avoid them.

Error vs Fix
MISMATCHED ABI/ADDRESS
Ensure ABI and address come from the same deploy output
MISSING SIGNER
Require wallet connection before writes and use contract.connect(signer)
HARD-CODING PRIVATE KEYS
Always use injected wallets; never store keys in frontend code
Safety checklist
  • Validate inputs before sending transactions to avoid reverts.
  • Show clear, localized error messages for wallet and RPC errors.
  • Test on a local node and verify network selection in the wallet.
Key Takeaway

Build safety and clarity into your UX so errors become actionable guidance rather than confusion.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the core ideas to remember. First, the ABI is the contract's JSON interface and is required to encode calls and decode results. Second, ethers. Contract represents the deployed contract and needs the address, ABI, and a Provider or Signer depending on the operation. Third, view and pure functions are read-only and require only a provider; writes need a signer and gas and you should await confirmation with tx. wait. Fourth, events let your DApp react in real time without heavy polling; register listeners carefully and remove them on cleanup. Fifth, implement clear error handling and never hardcode private keys in the frontend. These highlights form the practical checklist you will use when wiring a real DApp: deploy and copy ABI, instantiate contract, fetch reads, connect signer for writes, await confirmations, update UI from events, and handle errors gracefully. Keep this sequence in mind as you build and test your integration.

keyIdea.title: Three pillars
keyIdea.text: ABI, Provider/Signer, and Contract instance form the core of frontend contract interaction.

content.html:
What to Remember

Key Concepts

ABI
JSON description of functions and events used to encode and decode calls.
ethers.Contract
An object representing the deployed contract, instantiated with address, ABI, and provider or signer.
Read vs Write
Use a provider for view functions; connect a signer for state-changing transactions and await confirmation.
Summary Takeaway

These pieces together enable a predictable, user-friendly DApp that reads on-chain data, submits transactions securely, and updates in real time.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Compact reminders and the final takeaway

narration.text: A final compact reminder: always pair the ABI with the exact deployed address, use a provider for reads and a signer for writes, listen to events for responsive updates, and handle errors with clear, user-focused messages. Test the full flow locally with Hardhat, import the generated Greeter JSON into your frontend, and verify the wallet is on the same network. These practices reduce friction for users and lower the chance of confusing runtime errors. Consider these as a short checklist you can follow every time you wire a new contract into a frontend. Which checklist item will you add to your next DApp integration? What to Remember means abi + address, provider vs signer, tx.wait for confirmation, events for live ui, and robust error handling.. In practical terms, compact reminders and the final takeaway. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Final checklist
keyIdea.text: ABI + address, Provider vs Signer, tx.wait for confirmation, events for live UI, and robust error handling.

content.html:
Quick Reference

What to Remember

A final cheat sheet for wiring contracts into your frontend.

ABI & Address
Keep them together in a JSON artifact and update on redeploys.
Provider / Signer
Provider for reads, signer for writes; never sign transactions in app code.
Events & Errors
Listen for events to update UI and handle errors with friendly messages.
Final Takeaway

Follow the deployment and integration checklist to ensure reliable, secure, and user-friendly contract interactions.
